name: Naïve Realism
statement: People assume they see reality objectively and conclude that those who disagree must be uninformed, irrational, or biased.
meaning: In social psychology, naïve realism is the conviction that one perceives the world objectively, as it truly is. From this follows the expectation that other rational people, given the same facts, will share one's views, and that persistent disagreement signals the other side's ignorance, irrationality, or bias. It is a core driver of conflict and misunderstanding.
mechanism: Ross and Ward described three tenets: that I see the world objectively; that others will agree with me if they are reasonable and informed; and that if they disagree, they must be uninformed, irrational, or biased. This "I'm objective, you're biased" asymmetry sustains related phenomena like the bias blind spot, false consensus, and the hostile media effect.

examples.text: In Vallone, Ross, and Lepper (1985), pro-Israeli and pro-Arab students watched the same news coverage of the Sabra and Shatila massacre and each side perceived it as biased against their own position.
Pronin, Lin, and Ross (2002) found people readily see biases in others while judging themselves comparatively free of bias.
Partisans often assume opponents are not merely mistaken but ill-informed or acting in bad faith, rather than seeing the same facts differently.

whyItMatters: Naïve realism helps explain intractable disagreement, polarization, and failed negotiation, since each side treats its own view as simple fact. Recognizing it is a lever for conflict resolution and perspective-taking.
limits: It is a tendency, not an absolute; people can and do recognize the constructed, perspectival nature of their views, especially with training or reflection. The strength of the effect varies by issue involvement and context, and the psychological usage should not be conflated with the older philosophical doctrine of the same name.
misreadings: It is not the philosophical claim that perception directly reflects reality; here it names a false confidence in one's own objectivity.
origin: Social psychologists Lee Ross and Andrew Ward developed the concept in the 1990s.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Naïve realism (psychology)" article — supports the definition, the three tenets from Ross and Ward, the 1990s development, and links to the hostile media and bias blind spot findings.
Wikipedia's "Hostile media effect" article — supports the Vallone, Ross, and Lepper (1985) study in which opposing partisans each saw identical coverage as biased against them.
